source_read: PDF PDFs/Cocaine/Butler_2017_CrackHealthOutcomesSRMA.pdf, the accepted manuscript: 82 PDF pages, an unnumbered cover page and then manuscript pages printed 'Page 1 of 81' to 'Page 81 of 81' (PDF page = manuscript page + 1). Pages are cited as 'PDF p. N (manuscript p. N-1)'. Whole text read from my own pdftotext extraction; PDF pp. 5, 8, 9, 10, 17, 19, 22 and the tables and figures (PDF pp. 69-81: Figure 1, Figures 2 and 4, Table 2, Table 3) checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi (Table 2 pp. 75-76 at 110 dpi), Figure 3 at 300 dpi. Supplemental files 1-5 are not on file and were not read.

claims.overstatement: The Butler sentence is accurate in its facts: 302 included articles (302 studies in the PRISMA qualitative synthesis); pooled comparisons were against non-drug users or the general population, never powder; crack against other cocaine use was mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies cited) and showed no difference for 10 diagnoses (5 studies cited); none of this was pooled. Four wording points. (1) 'none of them was pooled or tested' should read that the review neither pooled nor tested them: the primary studies ran their own analyses (Chen and Anthony 2004, one of the 12, reports intervals). (2) The authors call crack use a 'facilitator or marker' for risk behaviours or risk environments; dropping 'facilitator' narrows what they allow. (3) The opening framing, that the sources describe the differences as route, amounts and circumstances 'rather than a property of crack itself', goes further than Butler: the review names crack's distinct pharmacology alongside routes of administration and users' marginalization as possible explanations (PDF p. 5), lists 'pharmacological source' and alkaloid cocaine crossing the placenta among untested pathways (Table 3), leaves direct drug effects open for neonatal outcomes, and calls causation unclear for mental health (PDF pp. 21-22). Its rule-out of a direct cause is limited to infections and violence. (4) The claim's summary of the crack-versus-other-cocaine comparisons omits single-study differences that Butler reports in both directions: more anorexia and insomnia and less suicide ideation among people using crack than among other people using cocaine; more violence against others than intranasal use but not injection (one study). The claim does not overstate Butler's numbers.
claims.note: Partly supported as far as Butler goes: every Butler-specific number and attribution checks out on the rendered pages. The part not supported by Butler is the framing that the differences are not a property of crack itself, which Butler leaves open outside infections and violence. The two counts (12 and 5) are citation counts in one paragraph, recounted from the printed list; the 10 diagnoses are also recounted. The review counts 302 articles, not studies (the PRISMA box says studies).

anchors.locator: 3.2 Narrative Synthesis > 3.2.2 Mental and Behavioural Disorders, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Crack compared with other cocaine use, narrative synthesis only: evidence described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies cited, among them Chen and Anthony 2004 and Gawin and Kleber 1986); no difference in prevalence reported for 10 diagnoses (ADHD, antisocial personality disorder, bipolar disorders, dysthymia, eating disorders, mania, obsessive-compulsive disorder, psychosis symptoms, PTSD, substance-induced disorders; 5 studies cited). No effect sizes and no pooled estimate or test by the review.

anchors.locator: 3.2 Narrative Synthesis > 3.2.2 Mental and Behavioural Disorders, 3rd paragraph (first sentence)
anchors.extracted: Among people who used cocaine, crack use was positively associated with anorexia and insomnia (1 study, Schwartz et al. 1991) and negatively associated with suicide ideation (1 study, Paim Kessler et al. 2012). Single-study differences in both directions that the claim's summary of the crack-versus-other-cocaine comparisons leaves out.

anchors.page: PDF p. 9 (manuscript p. 8); PDF p. 79 (manuscript p. 78)
anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.2 Data Extraction, Analysis and Quality Control, 4th paragraph; Table 3 caption
anchors.extracted: Meta-analyses were run only where at least 3 studies had sufficiently comparable comparison groups of non-drug users or the general population (random effects, Stata 14.1); Table 3 summarizes crack use compared to the general population. No meta-analysis compares crack with powder or other cocaine.

anchors.page: PDF p. 10 (manuscript p. 9); PDF p. 69 (manuscript p. 68)
anchors.extracted: 4,700 records screened, 1,415 full texts assessed, 400 articles extracted, 302 articles included (302 studies in the qualitative synthesis), 79 studies in the meta-analyses (24 meta-analyses).

anchors.locator: 4. Discussion, 4th paragraph (the paragraph begins on PDF p. 21)
anchors.extracted: For STIs, HIV or HCV infection, and experiencing or committing violence, the authors judge crack not a plausible direct causal agent; crack use likely acts as a facilitator or marker for risk behaviours (shared paraphernalia, high-risk sex) or for exposure to risk environments (violent drug markets, sex work).

anchors.page: PDF p. 21 (manuscript p. 20); PDF p. 22 (manuscript p. 21)
anchors.extracted: Outside infections and violence the authors do not rule out a direct effect: poor neonatal outcomes with maternal crack use may come from direct drug effects (alkaloid cocaine crossing the placenta) or indirect ones (malnutrition, lack of healthcare); for mental health it is unclear whether crack use is causative, reactive or comorbid.

Crack is made by heating powder cocaine with a base (often sodium bicarbonate) into a more combustible alkaline product, typically smoked. Its use is concentrated in young, socio-economically marginalized (poor, homeless) urban populations, mostly in the Americas. Risks that appear distinct from those of cocaine use are put down, as possibilities, to crack's distinct pharmacology and routes of administration, or to users' predominantly marginalized status and distinct behaviours and exposures; none of these is tested.

People who use crack are described as among the poorest, least educated, most disadvantaged and criminalized, yet commonly youngest, people who use drugs in their settings; this marginalization is presumed to contribute strongly to risk pathways such as experiencing and perpetrating violence, and to disconnection from prevention, treatment and health services.

anchors.locator: 3.2 Narrative Synthesis > 3.2.5 Harm to Others: Violence, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: One study (Giannini et al. 1993): people using crack were more likely to report violence against others than people using cocaine intranasally, but not more than people injecting cocaine. No consistent relation between crack use and violence against others overall, in general populations or among other people who use drugs.

Pathways listed by the authors, none tested: dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances (5 articles, not significant, grade D), binge use of crack; mortality (3 articles, positive, grade C), rapid absorption causing fatal acute intoxication at lower doses than other routes, and chronic disease; violence against others (2 articles, positive, grade D), aggression, social construct, financial constraints, criminality, pharmacological source; maternal and neonatal outcomes, vasoconstriction, socio-demographic risks, teratogenic properties of cocaine, alkaloid cocaine easily crossing the placenta, acute intoxication.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.1 Search Strategy and Selection Criteria, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Crack use was counted wherever studies referred to crack, freebase or alkaloid cocaine, or smoked cocaine; mixed drug-using groups were included if at least 75% reported crack use (example given: a cocaine group 86% of whom used crack). The review's crack group is therefore defined by the smokable form and route and can include some people who did not use crack.

anchors.page: PDF p. 24 (manuscript p. 23); PDF p. 4 (manuscript p. 3)
anchors.locator: 4.1 Limitations, 2nd paragraph; Abstract, Results and Conclusions
anchors.extracted: Because cross-sectional studies were included, health problems could precede crack use and drive it. Most underlying research was of limited or poor quality, with crack often a secondary covariate. The abstract's conclusion says it is unclear whether crack has a direct causal effect, whether risk factors interact, or whether an outside factor drives both crack use and the outcomes.

All values and study counts match Table 2 on the rendered pages.
3.2.1 paragraphs 2, 3, 5 and 8 (manuscript pp. 12-14) say what the card says.
Anxiety is marked '+' in Table 2 on the rendered page (manuscript p. 76) although 0.81-1.76 includes 1.

Counts recounted from the printed citation lists: 12 and 5 studies, 10 diagnoses. 'None of these comparisons was pooled or tested' is right for the review (no pooling, no test of its own); the primary studies, Chen and Anthony 2004 among them, did report their own estimates, so the sentence should say 'by the review'.

Grades checked row by row in Table 3 on the rendered pages; no grade A.
The sentence on infections and violence is on manuscript p. 21 (PDF p. 22); the paragraph starts on manuscript p. 20, so 'pp. 20-21' is right.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract (manuscript p. 2): 'Conclusive evidence and meta-analyses'; 3.3 and Conclusions say substantial; Table 3 grades B.
Table 2 '4', Figure 4 seven rows, Table 3 '6' all seen on the rendered pages.

Recomputed from Figure 3: double-counted infants 55 + 483 + 42 = 580 exposed and 55 + 3158 + 56 = 3,269 controls; 1,089 + 747 = 1,836 and 3,750 + 4,389 = 8,139; Fulroth controls 12/985 (1.2%); subgroups 2.37 (1.84-3.07) and 2.22 (1.68-2.92); upper limit 2.77 in the figure against 2.78 in Table 2.

The core point stands: the four reasons for the 98 articles excluded after data extraction (35, 25, 18, 18) sum to 96. But 'clips most exclusion reasons' overstates it. Word positions in the text layer put 14 reasons in the three exclusion boxes, and 7 of them are visible on the printed figure: 2975 not relevant; 333, 275, 177 and 163 (the word 'appropriate' clipped); 35 and 25. The other 7 are hidden: 269 duplicates and 41 unable to access in the title-abstract box (2,975 + 269 + 41 = 3,285, as printed), 32 not quantitative, 25 duplicates and 10 no full-text access in the full-text box (333 + 275 + 177 + 163 + 32 + 25 + 10 = 1,015, as printed), and 18 and 18 after data extraction. Only the post-extraction box fails to add up. The card's 'attrition' field ('most of the reasons are clipped') and AMSTAR 2 item 7 note need the same change.

Table 2 cites 'Supplemental file 2: Figure N' throughout; the text (manuscript pp. 9, 11) puts the remaining forest plots in Supplemental file 4 and the grading criteria in file 2 (manuscript pp. 8-9, 81).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: items 7, 9 and 11 (critical) not met, as the card says. Item 13 'yes' is generous given that no study-level appraisal was done, but this does not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'conclusive' in the abstract against grade B in Table 3; mortality graded C while the Discussion calls mortality data a major gap; the cardiovascular statement in 3.3 is not borne out by Table 3.

missed: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 5, manuscript p. 4): the authors put crack-specific risks down, as possibilities, to crack's 'distinct pharmacology and routes of administration' or to users' marginalized status and distinct behaviours and exposures. This bears directly on the crack-versus-powder claim, which says the sources describe differences as not a property of crack itself. The card mentions distinct pharmacology only in a timeline entry for Hatsukami 1996.

Table 3 'Potential risk pathways' (manuscript pp. 78-80): untested hypotheses mixing route (rapid absorption at lower doses than other routes for mortality; inhalation of burning particulate), pattern (binge use for dependence), drug (vasoconstriction, 'pharmacological source' for violence against others, alkaloid cocaine crossing the placenta) and social factors (lifestyle, marginalization). The card's note on key finding 12 records only the binge-use pathway.

Discussion, 4th paragraph (manuscript p. 20): for neonatal outcomes the authors allow direct drug effects as well as indirect ones; their rule-out of a direct cause covers only infections and violence. Key finding 13 covers mental health but not this.
Minor inconsistency: premature birth is defined as 37 weeks or earlier in 3.1.3 and Table 2 (manuscript pp. 10, 77) but as under 37 weeks in Table 3 (manuscript p. 80).
